stem: The order database needs a four-hour outage to patch, and the business owner refuses a window during peak season. Which response is best?

options.text: Agree an off-peak window and add a compensating control meanwhile
Patch during peak season because security outranks operations
Close the finding as a false positive so it leaves the report
Leave it unfixed and remove it from future reports

explanation: The analyst should work with the owner on a safe window and reduce risk in the meantime. Forcing the outage ignores business impact, and hiding or mislabeling the finding removes accountability.

stem: Which TWO are benefits of tracking remediation status in a ticketing system?

options.text: Visibility of overdue items so they can be followed up
Automatic removal of every vulnerability once a ticket exists
An auditable history of who fixed what and when
No further need to rescan after a fix is reported
A guarantee that patches never cause downtime

explanation: A tracker keeps evidence and shows what is late. Creating a ticket fixes nothing, validation is still required, and patch downtime cannot be guaranteed away.

stem: Which TWO are inhibitors to remediation?

options.text: Frequent scanner signature updates from the vendor
A critical business process that cannot tolerate downtime
Credentialed scanning being enabled on servers
A dashboard that uses a dark color theme
A contract that limits changes to a vendor-managed appliance

explanation: Contractual limits on changes and business processes that cannot stop both delay fixes. Signature updates, credentialed scans and dashboard themes do not prevent anyone from remediating.

stem: A scorecard lists ten hosts with the same critical flaw. Two are internet-facing payroll servers and eight are isolated test systems. How should the action plan order the work?

options.text: Treat all ten hosts identically, because the severity score is the same for each
Fix the two internet-facing payroll servers first, then the test systems
Start with the test systems because they are easiest to patch
Defer all ten findings until the next scheduled quarterly review meeting

explanation: Exposure and business value raise priority when severity is equal. Ignoring context, choosing by convenience, or deferring critical findings all increase risk.

stem: Which TWO compensating controls reduce exposure of a server that cannot be patched?

options.text: Extending password reuse windows for the server accounts
Removing the server from vulnerability scan scope
Network segmentation that limits who can reach the server
Disabling audit logging on the server to save disk space
An intrusion prevention rule that blocks known exploit traffic

explanation: Segmentation and a virtual-patching rule reduce the chance of exploitation without changing the host. Longer password reuse, hiding the server from scans and turning off logs raise or conceal risk.

stem: After a fix is applied, what should happen before the finding is closed in the tracker?

options.text: The original scan report is deleted from the archive
A rescan confirms the vulnerability no longer exists
The asset is given a lower criticality rating by its owner
The ticket waits one full year before it can be closed

explanation: Validation proves the fix worked and gives auditors evidence. Deleting reports destroys the record, lowering criticality changes risk without fixing it, and a one-year wait has no basis.

stem: A fix is unavailable and the cost of mitigation exceeds the risk. What should accompany the decision to leave the finding open?

options.text: A verbal comment from the analyst that the risk seems low
Hiding the finding in the dashboard so that it no longer displays to anyone
A documented, time-limited risk acceptance signed by the business owner, with a review date
A note labelling the finding a false positive in the tracker

explanation: Accepting risk needs a written, approved and periodically reviewed decision by the person who owns the risk. Hiding the finding or relabeling it as a false positive misrepresents the situation.

stem: An auditor at a payment processor asks for evidence that scans run regularly and that findings are fixed. Which report best supports this?

options.text: A threat intelligence summary of the adversary groups active in the sector
An executive briefing about reputational damage after past incidents at other firms
A compliance report with scan dates, scope, findings and remediation status mapped to PCI DSS requirements
A log of firewall rule changes made during the past week

explanation: Auditors need dated, scoped evidence tied to the standard. Threat summaries, reputational briefings and firewall change logs do not show scan cadence or closure.

stem: A partner organization manages a shared gateway under a signed memorandum of understanding, and any change to it needs the partner agreement. Which inhibitor to remediation applies?

options.text: Legacy system
Degrading functionality
Business process interruption
Memorandum of understanding

explanation: A written agreement that gives another party a say over changes is an MOU inhibitor. Nothing here is out of support, nothing breaks when patched, and no downtime is described.

stem: A vendor stopped issuing patches for the operating system on a plant-floor workstation, so the flaw cannot be fixed. Which inhibitor to remediation is this?

options.text: Legacy system
Memorandum of understanding
Organizational governance
Business process interruption

explanation: Software or hardware past end of support, with no vendor fixes, is a legacy system problem. An MOU is an agreement between parties, governance is an approval or policy hurdle, and business process interruption is about downtime.

stem: Which THREE are typical stakeholders in a vulnerability remediation plan?

options.text: Unrelated external competitors
Anonymous participants in public forums
Business unit leaders accountable for the risk
Staff of the scanner vendor marketing department
Security analysts and engineers
System owners

explanation: Owners fix, analysts and engineers guide and verify, and business leaders own the risk. Competitors, forum users and vendor marketing have no role in the plan.

stem: A hosting contract guarantees 99.99 percent uptime, and applying a patch to the database cluster would need a reboot that breaks that guarantee. Which inhibitor to remediation does this describe?

options.text: Service-level agreement
Legacy system
Proprietary system
Organizational governance

explanation: A contractual uptime commitment that a fix would violate is an SLA constraint. The system is still supported and customer-managed, so it is not legacy or proprietary, and no approval policy is mentioned.

stem: A dashboard shows a 95 percent on-time remediation rate, yet auditors found several critical systems long overdue. What is the most likely flaw in the metric?

options.text: It was computed against the number of scan templates instead of the number of hosts
It treats a scan that finds nothing as an overdue finding
It blends every severity, so many low findings hide the overdue critical ones
It uses a different scoring version than the one the auditors use

explanation: A blended rate lets large volumes of easy, low-severity fixes mask late critical items, so the KPI should be reported per severity. The other explanations do not account for a high overall rate alongside overdue critical systems.

stem: A system owner declines a fix because policy requires data-owner approval for any downtime, and that approval has not been given. Which inhibitor to remediation is this?

options.text: Legacy system
Proprietary system
Organizational governance
Business process interruption

explanation: A policy or approval process that blocks action is an organizational governance inhibitor. The system is supported and customer-managed, and the blocker is an approval rule rather than the downtime itself.

stem: Which TWO belong in an executive summary of vulnerability posture?

options.text: Complete plugin output for each assessed host
The top exposures, their business impact and the decisions needed
The risk trend over time compared with the targets
Every raw packet captured during the scans
The command lines used to patch each host

explanation: Leaders need direction against targets and the exposures that call for decisions. Plugin output, packet data and command lines are detail for engineers.

stem: A library fix requires updating an application that another team owns, and a release freeze begins on Friday. What should the remediation plan record?

options.text: The dependency, the owning team and the dates, plus a compensating control until the release
Only the library version number, with the other team left out of the plan entirely
Nothing, because a release freeze waives all open findings
A request to delete the application from the asset inventory

explanation: Dependencies and their owners and dates make the plan actionable, and interim mitigation covers the gap. Ignoring the other team, assuming a waiver or deleting the asset leaves the risk unmanaged.

stem: Which visual is best for showing executives how the number of open findings changes over several weeks?

options.text: A table of registry settings from each scanned server
A tree view of the raw scanner output files in XML
A diagram of the packets exchanged during one scan
A line chart of open findings by severity over time

explanation: A trend line lets leaders see direction and progress at a glance. Registry tables, raw XML and packet diagrams are technical detail that does not show change over time to a non-technical audience.

stem: Which TWO items belong in a vulnerability remediation action plan?

options.text: A named owner and target date for each fix
The source code of the scanner plugins that found each flaw
The names and attribution of suspected attacker groups
Compensating controls for findings that cannot yet be patched
The scanner license invoices and renewal dates

explanation: An actionable plan assigns ownership and deadlines and covers interim safeguards for unpatchable items. Plugin source code, attribution and license paperwork do not help anyone fix a finding.

stem: Why does each finding in a remediation tracker list a named owner?

options.text: It tells the scanner which credentials to use for authenticated checks
It sets the base score of the finding from the owner role
It creates accountability for completing the fix by the agreed date
It chooses which signature set the scanner loads next

explanation: A named owner means someone is answerable for the fix and its due date. Scan credentials, scoring and signature selection are configured elsewhere.

stem: A report shows open critical findings falling each month while newly discovered critical findings stay flat and scan coverage is unchanged. What does this most likely indicate?

options.text: The scanner signatures are outdated and are missing recent flaws
Attackers have stopped targeting the environment this quarter
Remediation is outpacing discovery, so the backlog is shrinking
Asset owners are closing tickets without applying any fix

explanation: With steady discovery and coverage, a falling open count means fixes are being completed faster than new findings arrive. The other readings are not supported by the data given.

stem: Why does a risk scorecard factor in asset criticality as well as the severity score of a finding?

options.text: Criticality changes the base metrics that the scanner records for each flaw it detects
The same flaw poses more risk on a revenue-critical server than on a lab machine
Severity scores cannot be calculated for flaws found on production servers
Lab machines are never scanned, so their severity is always unknown

explanation: Business context decides how much damage exploitation could do, so the scorecard weights it. Asset criticality does not alter the base score, production servers are scored normally, and lab machines can be scanned.

stem: Which TWO are valid reasons to escalate a stalled remediation to senior management?

options.text: A low-severity finding on a test server was opened this week
A scan finished faster than it did last month
A critical finding is past its policy deadline with no mitigation in place
An analyst prefers a different report template for the team
A system owner refuses to fix a flaw and no risk acceptance has been signed

explanation: Escalation is warranted when serious risk is unmanaged or an owner blocks action without an approved exception. A new low finding, a fast scan and a template preference are routine matters.

stem: A legacy programmable logic controller cannot be patched. Which action best reduces the risk until the device is replaced?

options.text: Remove it from scan scope so the finding stops appearing
Lower its CVSS score in the scanner to match the lack of an available patch
Turn off logging on the device to cut down on noise
Isolate it on its own network segment with tightly limited access

explanation: Segmentation limits who can reach the flaw, which is a compensating control. Removing it from scope hides the risk, editing the score misstates it, and disabling logs reduces visibility.

stem: Several findings come from staff who build servers by hand and reuse weak administrator passwords. Which element of the action plan best addresses the root cause?

options.text: A longer scan interval for those servers during the next quarter
A lower reporting threshold for those findings in the dashboard
A new signature set loaded on the scanner each week
Awareness and training for the staff who build the servers

explanation: The cause is human practice, so training on secure builds fixes it at the source. Changing scan timing, thresholds or signatures only affects detection or reporting.

stem: A newly disclosed flaw has no patch yet and is being exploited. What should the report to executives emphasize?

options.text: A detailed step-by-step account of how the exploit technique works in practice
Which assets are exposed, the interim mitigations in place and the expected fix date
A statement that no exposure exists until the vendor ships a patch
A list of every vulnerability the team closed during the last year, by month

explanation: Leaders need exposure, protection now and timing. Exploit mechanics are too technical, claiming no exposure is false, and last year closures do not inform the current decision.

stem: A security appliance is sold as a sealed unit. The customer cannot change its operating system, and the vendor ships fixes on its own schedule. Which inhibitor to remediation applies?

options.text: Proprietary system
Degrading functionality
Legacy system
Service-level agreement

explanation: A vendor-controlled platform that the customer cannot modify is a proprietary system. Degrading functionality concerns a fix that breaks features, legacy means out of support, and an SLA sets service commitments.

stem: What is the main purpose of vulnerability management reporting?

options.text: To replace the detection logic that is built into the scanner itself
To guarantee that no known vulnerability can ever be exploited
To store every packet that the scanner sent during each scan window
To turn scan findings into information that supports risk decisions

explanation: Reports translate raw findings into risk, priorities and actions that people can decide on. They do not replace scanner logic, cannot guarantee that nothing is exploitable, and are not a store of packet data.

stem: Which TWO should a technical remediation report for system engineers include?

options.text: Board-level discussion of insurance coverage
A draft press release about the exposure
Charts comparing the company to its competitors
Specific fix steps or patch references
The affected hosts and software versions

explanation: Engineers need to know what is affected and how to fix it. Insurance discussion, press drafts and competitor charts serve other audiences.

stem: A compliance report from the vulnerability management program is mainly meant to show which of the following?

options.text: How many new exploits were published against the vendor products this quarter alone
Which adversary groups are currently targeting the organization sector
How quickly the help desk closes ordinary user tickets during a month
Whether systems and processes meet the requirements of a regulation or standard

explanation: A compliance report demonstrates accountability against a regulation or standard, such as scan frequency and remediation status. Exploit counts and adversary activity belong to threat intelligence, and help desk speed is an IT service metric.

stem: Why would a report highlight the most common vulnerabilities across the environment?

options.text: To reveal patterns, like one outdated component, that one fix could remove everywhere
To rank individual staff members by how many configuration mistakes they made on builds
To prove that scanning was switched off on the busiest production servers
To avoid the need for a risk score on each individual asset

explanation: Recurring findings point to a shared root cause, such as an old library in a standard image, so one change fixes many hosts. The report is not a staff ranking, evidence of disabled scans, or a substitute for per-asset risk.

stem: In testing, a security patch breaks a plug-in that the finance application depends on. Which inhibitor to remediation does this describe?

options.text: Organizational governance
Degrading functionality
Memorandum of understanding
Proprietary system

explanation: When a fix would reduce or break needed functionality, degrading functionality is the inhibitor. Governance is an approval hurdle, an MOU is an agreement with another party, and nothing says the platform is vendor-locked.

stem: The same finding keeps reappearing in reports after being closed on several servers. What does this most suggest?

options.text: The scanner has permanently stopped working on those particular servers
The finding was a false positive from the start
The root cause, such as a flawed build image, was never corrected
The servers have been removed from the asset inventory

explanation: A recurring finding points to a source that keeps reintroducing it, such as an outdated golden image. A stopped scanner or a removed asset would not produce repeated reports, and a false positive would not be closed as fixed.

stem: Which content best fits a monthly vulnerability report written for an executive audience?

options.text: Raw plugin output for every host that the scanner assessed during the month, with all fields
Overall risk trend, the business impact of the top exposures and the decisions or resources needed
Per-host patch command lines and configuration file differences
The full list of scanner signature identifiers loaded for the scan

explanation: Executives need risk, impact and the decisions required, in plain language. Raw output, command lines and signature lists suit engineers and would bury the message.

stem: A flaw affects software in a hospital infusion pump. Who must be involved in the remediation plan beyond the security team?

options.text: The device vendor, clinical engineering and the clinicians who use the pumps
Only the marketing team and the public relations office for the whole hospital group
Only the scanner vendor sales representative and a reseller
Only the accounts payable team in the finance department

explanation: Fixing a medical device needs the manufacturer, the engineers who maintain it and the users affected by any downtime. The other groups have no role in the fix.

stem: Which part of a remediation action plan records approved baselines and tracks changes so that fixes can be verified later?

options.text: Configuration management
Risk acceptance documents
Awareness training sessions
Compensating control design

explanation: Configuration management keeps authoritative baselines and a change record that proves what was changed and when. Risk acceptance, training and compensating controls serve other purposes in the plan.

stem: A report shows the percentage of critical findings closed within the window that policy sets. What is this kind of measure?

options.text: An indicator of compromise for the affected hosts on the network
A compensating control applied to systems that remain unpatched
A false positive rate for the scanner signatures
A key performance indicator for remediation timeliness

explanation: The percentage closed on time is a KPI that shows how well the remediation process meets its targets. An indicator of compromise describes attacker evidence, a compensating control is a safeguard, and a false positive rate measures scanner accuracy.

stem: Which THREE are common vulnerability management KPIs?

options.text: Count of phishing emails blocked by the mail gateway
Average password length across the directory
Mean time to remediate
Number of badge readers installed in the building
Number of open critical findings
Percentage of findings closed within the policy window

explanation: Time to fix, open critical counts and on-time closure all describe the remediation process. The other measures belong to email security, identity hygiene and physical security.

stem: Which measure best shows whether remediation is getting faster over time?

options.text: The total number of scans that were launched in each calendar month
Mean time to remediate, tracked by severity over several months
The count of plugins enabled in the scan policy
The number of times managers opened the dashboard

explanation: Mean time to remediate directly measures speed from discovery to fix, and tracking it by severity shows the trend. Scan counts, plugin counts and dashboard views measure activity, not remediation speed.

stem: Which TWO are limitations of relying on the base severity score alone in a report?

options.text: It cannot be calculated for any flaw found in a web application
It changes every time the scanner service restarts
It applies only to flaws on operating systems
It does not reflect how valuable the affected asset is to the business
It does not show whether exploitation is happening in the wild

explanation: A base score is fixed and generic, so asset value and live exploitation must come from other inputs. It can be calculated for web flaws, does not vary with restarts, and covers many software types.

stem: Which TWO actions help when a security patch fails testing because it degrades application functionality?

options.text: Deploy the patch to production anyway and repair problems afterward
Apply a compensating control while the fix is validated
Work with the vendor on a compatible fix after testing in staging
Mark the finding resolved because a patch exists
Disable the staging environment so the failure stops appearing

explanation: Resolve the incompatibility properly and cover the gap meanwhile. Forcing the patch risks outages, a patch that is not applied is not a resolution, and removing staging only hides test failures.

stem: The table shows one month of remediation activity for the example.internal environment. Use it to answer each question.

payload.caption: Findings by severity for the month

fields.label: Critical findings still open at month end
Share of closed High findings that met the SLA
Severity with the lowest on-time closure rate

options.text: Critical
High
Medium

fields.label: Findings of all severities still open at month end

explanation: Open at end equals open at start plus new minus closed. Critical is 20 + 12 - 25 = 7. High on-time is 30 of 40, or 75 percent, which is lower than Critical (20 of 25, 80 percent), Medium (54 of 60, 90 percent) and Low (100 percent).

partExplanations.high: 30 closed within the SLA out of 40 closed is 30 / 40 = 75 percent.
partExplanations.worst: On-time rates are Critical 80, High 75, Medium 90 and Low 100 percent, so High is lowest.
partExplanations.total: Critical 7, High 35, Medium 70 and Low 110 add up to 222 open findings.

stem: Match each audience to the vulnerability report content that serves it best.

choices.text: Risk trend against targets and the decisions needed
Per-host fix steps and software versions
Dated scan evidence and closure records for a standard
Affected components and dependencies to plan a release
Mean time to remediate and on-time closure by severity

explanation: Each audience needs a different level of detail: executives want risk and decisions, engineers want actions, auditors want evidence, application owners want impact and dependencies, and the program lead tracks process KPIs.

partExplanations.p1: Leaders act on risk trend and required decisions, not technical detail.
partExplanations.p2: Administrators apply fixes, so they need hosts, versions and steps.
partExplanations.p3: Auditors need dated proof that scans ran and findings were closed.
partExplanations.p4: Application owners schedule changes around what is affected and what it depends on.
partExplanations.p5: The program lead watches remediation speed and timeliness measures.

stem: Sort each item into the category it belongs to in a vulnerability management report or action plan.

items.text: Vendor-managed appliance the customer cannot modify
Intrusion prevention rule blocking exploit traffic
Percentage of critical findings closed within the SLA
Operating system past end of vendor support
Count of open findings by severity

explanation: Inhibitors are the obstacles that delay a fix, compensating controls lower risk while a fix is delayed, and metrics measure progress.

partExplanations.i1: A sealed vendor platform is a proprietary-system obstacle.
partExplanations.i2: A downtime freeze is a business process interruption obstacle.
partExplanations.i3: A blocking rule reduces exposure without patching, so it compensates.
partExplanations.i4: Limiting who can reach the server compensates for the missing patch.
partExplanations.i5: It measures how long fixes take, so it is a metric.
partExplanations.i6: It measures timeliness against policy, so it is a metric.
partExplanations.i7: No vendor fixes exist for an unsupported system, a legacy obstacle.
partExplanations.i8: Counts by severity track the size of the backlog, so they are a metric.

stem: Review this entry from a remediation action plan. Select every element that leaves the plan not actionable.

nodes.text: Fix: apply vendor update 4.2.1 to web tier

spots.name: Fix: apply vendor update 4.2.1 to web tier

explanation: An actionable plan names an owner, identifies exactly which hosts are affected, and includes a way to verify the fix. The due date, the specific fix and the severity are already clear.

partExplanations.owner: Without an owner nobody is accountable for the fix.
partExplanations.hosts: All servers is too vague to schedule or verify work.
partExplanations.valid: No validation means the fix is never confirmed.

stem: A legacy human-machine interface at a plant cannot be patched. Configure its entry in the action plan.

options.text: Apply the newest vendor patch to the live system now
Apply compensating controls and document the risk acceptance
Remove the system from scan scope
Legacy system
Organizational governance
Degrading functionality
Time-limited, with a scheduled review date
Permanent, with no further review
Cleared automatically after the next scan

fields.label: Who signs off on the residual risk

options.text: The owner of the business process
The scanner administrator
The help desk lead

explanation: The device has no available fix, so the plan lowers risk with compensating controls and a documented acceptance. The obstacle is a legacy system, the exception must be time-limited and reviewed, and the process owner accepts the risk.

partExplanations.approach: With no patch possible, compensating controls plus documented acceptance manage the risk; hiding it from scans does not.
partExplanations.inhibitor: A system without vendor fixes is a legacy-system obstacle.
partExplanations.review: Exceptions need an expiry and review so the risk is revisited.
partExplanations.signoff: The person who owns the business process owns the residual risk.

stem: Complete the reporting flow. Place the best output for each need named below the components.

zones.name: Give engineers a per-host list of fixes to apply
Show leaders how open findings trend against targets
Give auditors proof of scan frequency and closure
Confirm that a completed fix removed the flaw

labels.text: Ticket queue with owner and due date
Dashboard with trend lines by severity
Compliance report with dated scan evidence
Follow-up rescan of the affected host
Raw packet capture from the scan window
Attribution brief on an adversary group

explanation: Each output serves a need: a ticket queue assigns fixes, a trend dashboard informs leaders, a dated compliance report satisfies auditors, and a rescan validates the fix. Packet captures and attribution briefs are not vulnerability reporting outputs.

partExplanations.z1: A ticket queue gives engineers owned, dated work items.
partExplanations.z2: Trend lines by severity show progress against targets for leaders.
partExplanations.z3: A dated compliance report is the evidence auditors ask for.
partExplanations.z4: Only a rescan confirms the vulnerability is gone.

stem: Put the steps of tracking a finding through remediation in order, starting when a scan result arrives. Each step needs the result of the step before it.

steps.text: Test and apply the fix or a compensating control
Report the outcome and close the ticket
Prioritize the finding using severity and asset criticality
Rescan to validate that the flaw is gone
Assign an owner and agree a deadline in the action plan

explanation: Priority sets the deadline, the owner then performs the fix, validation checks the fix, and only then is the result reported and the ticket closed.

partExplanations.0: Priority decides how urgent the work is and who must be involved.
partExplanations.1: The deadline comes from the priority, and an owner is needed before work starts.
partExplanations.2: The owner applies the fix once the plan exists.
partExplanations.3: Validation can only happen after a fix has been applied.
partExplanations.4: Closure and reporting rest on validated results.
